item.title: Family Portrait
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
The Patient Wren had surveyed for eleven turns when it found the world every settler in the Reach dreams of.

Dessa Oru, the youngest reader on the team, kept the scans open on her wrist long after she should have closed them. Seventy percent water. Moving plates. A star that had not flickered in four billion years.

“Perfect,” said Reckoner Varga, leaning over Dessa’s shoulder. “Water, warmth, a good heavy moon to keep the seasons steady. If you sat down to design a world for living things, you’d draw this one.”

item.title: Camp Ramesses
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Mars, 2057

The descent took seven minutes, and for every one of them, Commander Amara Okonkwo forgot to breathe.

Below the lander Perseverance II, the north polar plains of Mars rolled out like a rust-colored ocean, streaked with the white of ancient ice. It was the year 2057, nearly ninety years after the first boots touched the Moon, and a decade after the lunar colony had grown from a handful of domes into a proper town. Humanity was finally about to stand on another world.

item.title: Templar Heist
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: The midday sun hung over the Levant like an anvil, baking the cracked earth into fine white dust. Through the shimmer of the heat haze, a heavily guarded convoy rolled along a deserted trade road, bound for the coastal fortress at Acre. Iron-rimmed wheels groaned beneath the weight of three sturdy carriages, each packed with iron-bound chests of gold bullion being transferred from an inland Templar vault. Surrounding the cargo was a squad of twelve armored knights, their white surcoats bearing the crimson cross, swords glinting in the blinding glare.

item.title: Subject 207
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Sublevel Four

Dr. Elias Verhoeven had not seen the sun in eleven days, and he had stopped noticing. Down on Sublevel Four of the Halcyon Institute, the only light that mattered was the pale blue glow of the incubation chamber and the thin green line of a heartbeat on the monitor.

Eight years. Two hundred and six trials. He kept every name in his head. Marcus, whose heart simply stopped. Ines, whose muscles tore themselves from the bone. Some volunteers had come for the money. Others had come for the promise: a human being with no ceiling. Strength, speed, intellect, perception, every one at its maximum, all at once.

item.title: The Defence
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
There was no courtroom.

He had expected scales. A bridge. Fire somewhere off to the left. There was only a floor that was not a floor, a light with no source, and the sudden, total knowledge that he was known.

He tried to speak. His mouth would not open.

So his hands spoke instead.

His right hand went first, in his own voice, and it talked about the money — the small amounts, then the larger ones, then the signature that was not his. His feet named the doors they had carried him through. His skin testified last, and that was the worst of it, because skin remembers what the mind agrees to forget.

item.title: Reply All
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
The first one arrived on a Tuesday. Subject line: Re: Sunday long run — bring the gazebo poles.

I don’t run. I have never in my life owned a gazebo. I marked it as spam and forgot about it.

Four more came that week. Then a photograph: nine people in reflective vests standing in a car park under a sky the colour of wet cement, and underneath it, one line.

item.title: Farmer's Burden
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: Six months after the world collapsed into teeth and rot, the silence felt heavier than the stench of decay. Brother Thomas and his small flock of surviving clergy had spent half a year wandering through ash and ruin before stumbling upon a genuine miracle: a sprawling, untouched farmstead as green and vibrant as Eden. The farmer, a tall, quiet man with eyes like polished obsidian, greeted them at the edge of the timber. His terms were simple enough. They could shelter in the dry comfort of his barn for as long as they wished, provided they respected his boundary and never crossed his threshold uninvited.

item.title: Field Data
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Milo held his phone up to a maple tree and grinned as a shimmering fox made of blue light blinked into existence on his screen, sitting in the crook of a branch that, in the real world, held nothing at all.

Glimmer captured: Ember Fox. Collection: 214/300.

He’d been chasing this one for three days. The app had teased it near the reservoir, then the fountain, then finally here, on the gravel path that cut through Hollis Park. He snapped the photo, watched the little creature dissolve into a burst of pixel-confetti, and felt the small, stupid, wonderful joy of a thing checked off a list.

item.title: Cost of Infinite Power
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description:
Petty Officer Second Class Marcus Ibe stood at the rail as the destroyer came about, its wake curling white against water the color of gunmetal. Behind them, the strait narrowed toward the coast of Yemen, a smudge of brown hills he’d stared at for six months without ever setting foot on.

The order had come down at 0400: reposition east, out of range, hold formation with the carrier group. Not a retreat, the XO had said. A repositioning. Marcus had written the word in his notebook and circled it twice, like that might make it mean something else.

item.title: Iblis on Vacation
item.author: techjourneyman@gmail.com (techjourneyman)
item.description: The low, rhythmic thrum of the cruise liner’s engines vibrated through the deck floorboards, but it did nothing to soothe the tremor in Arthur’s soul. A parish priest of over twenty-five years, he had spent two decades delivering eulogies, sitting by hospice beds, and attempting to explain the unexplainable to shattered parents. His congregation believed he was on sabbatical for rest, but in truth, he had fled. Standing alone near the stern of the upper deck, he stared into the vast, pitch-black Atlantic, feeling completely hollowed out by the sheer volume of human agony he had been forced to shepherd.
